children: 0324 GMT - The latest meeting between President Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping is a "stability summit, not a breakthrough" one, according to Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo. "The extension [of a trade truce] lowers the risk of an immediate escalation, but it leaves companies facing much the same uncertainty about the rules they will operate under next year," Chanana says in a research note. Investors are looking for "practical" signals, such as published tariff changes, actual rare-earth shipments, agricultural purchases beyond existing soybean commitments, and any change to chip-export licenses, she says. The outcome looks "too thin to drive a sustained rerating of Chinese equities," she adds. (tracy.qu@wsj.com)

0320 GMT - The Singapore dollar consolidates against its U.S. counterpart, but prospects of rate increases by the Federal Reserve could weigh on the Asian currency. The U.S. dollar strengthened overnight, as the selloff in global bonds continued, Maybank analysts say in a report. Rising oil prices also add to inflation concerns and reinforce expectations that the Fed's tightening cycle may have further room to run, the analysts add. The U.S. dollar is flat at 1.2791 Singapore dollars, LSEG data show. (amanda.lee@wsj.com)

0313 GMT - Indonesia's GDP growth could moderate to 5.1% in 2H from 5.45% in 1H, mainly due to slower domestic consumption growth and a larger drag from net exports, RHB economist Wong Xian Yong says in a note. He keeps his 2026 GDP growth estimate at 5.2%, with investment expected to remain the main support as household spending cools. Strong investment in manufacturing, infrastructure and downstream industries should partly offset weaker consumption and external trade. Net exports are expected to keep dragging as imports of capital goods and raw materials outpace subdued exports. Government spending should continue to support domestic demand, although its growth contribution is expected to ease. Wong maintains his 2026 inflation forecast at 2.8%, with upside risks from higher food and energy prices toward year-end and into early 2027.(yingxian.wong@wsj.com)

0242 GMT - The Reserve Bank of Australia has concerns about both domestic and global inflation risks, but as it is likely to raise its policy rate next week, it should also be mulling the issue of stronger local GDP growth. Westpac economist Pat Bustamante expects 3Q GDP growth at 2.3% on year, up from 2.1% in 2Q. The economy is proving more resilient than previously feared, he adds. The RBA is unlikely to be comfortable with firmer economic momentum given that it is trying to engineer a period of below-trend growth to ensure inflation returns to its target, he says. (james.glynn@wsj.com; @JamesGlynnWSJ)

0222 GMT - The Reserve Bank of Australia has more work to do to tame inflation, and by the time it is done, the official cash rate should be at its highest level since 2008, says Adam Boyton, head of Australian economics at ANZ. The RBA will likely raise its policy rate next week and again in November, taking the official cash rate to 4.85%, he adds. The ongoing escalation of the conflict in the Middle East and the tendency of the RBA to view the rise in oil prices as much more of an inflation shock than a growth shock suggest the RBA is prepared to act, he says. (james.glynn@wsj.com; @JamesGlynnWSJ)

0158 GMT - Oxford Economics says its U.S. Business Cycle Indicator has dropped into recessionary territory, as higher energy prices squeeze real incomes and slowing immigration weigh on trend job growth. Still, it is questioning the data as a genuine recession signal because productivity growth is strong and the wealth effect is boosting consumer spending. Households aren't trading down to cheaper goods, a typical response in the lead-up to and aftermath of a recession, it adds. The artificial-intelligence build-out, elevated profit margins and tax cuts are also supporting investment, even as tariff and policy uncertainties persist, it says. (james.glynn@wsj.com; @JamesGlynnWSJ)

0140 GMT - The Reserve Bank of Australia has clearly grown very uneasy about inflation risks, and data next week are expected to show why. Taylor Nugent, an economist at National Australia Bank, expects headline inflation to bounce higher to 4.1% in August on higher fuel prices, from 3.5% in July. In quarterly terms, trimmed mean inflation is tracking higher than the RBA's August forecast of 0.83%, he adds. NAB is forecasting a 1.0% on-quarter trimmed mean outcome, with the risk skewed to a 1.1% result, he says. Significant uncertainty remains about the path forward for energy costs, but the cost shock already realized is very large, Nugent says. (james.glynn@wsj.com; @JamesGlynnWSJ)

0129 GMT - Asian currencies consolidate against the dollar in early trade. Treasury yields continued to set fresh multiyear highs Thursday, on expectations that the Fed will raise interest rates in October. "Oil is adding another layer of pressure to the rates story," says MUFG Bank's Lloyd Chan in a report. Renewed geopolitical risks in the Middle East against an already tight oil-market backdrop are raising concerns over supply and inflation, Chan adds. The U.S. dollar is 0.1% lower at 158.63 yen and 0.4% higher at 4.0670 Malaysian ringgit. The U.S. dollar is little changed at 1.2786 Singapore dollars, LSEG data show. (amanda.lee@wsj.com)

0116 GMT - Japanese government bond yields are higher following sharp gains in U.S. Treasury yields overnight, driven by strong U.S. economic data and expectations for the Fed's rate increases. The Fed's further tightening could accelerate the dollar's appreciation against the yen, which in turn raises speculation for the Bank of Japan's rate increases to mitigate upside risks in inflation. Investors are focusing on developments in the Middle East conflict and the U.S.-China summit meeting. The JGB yield curve is steeper. The 2-year yield is up 2 basis points at 1.920%, the 10-year yield is 3.5 basis points higher at 3.110%, and the 40-year yield is up 5.5 basis points at 4.255%. (kosaku.narioka@wsj.com; @kosakunarioka)

0035 GMT - The Reserve Bank of Australia is set to change focus next week. Three interest rate increases in the first half of the year were focused on correcting excessive easing in 2025. The likely increase in the official cash rate next week will be about global inflation risks, says Paul Bloxham, chief economist at HSBC, Australia. Part of the problem is also that inflation has already been high for an extended period--the trimmed mean has been above the 2.5% midpoint of the target band for 4.5 years, he adds. The RBA's reaction function is shifting, as it becomes less tolerant of high inflation, he says. (james.glynn@wsj.com; @JamesGlynnWSJ)

0020 GMT - Japanese stocks are higher, led by financial stocks following sharp gains in long-term U.S. Treasury yields overnight. Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group is up 2.5% and Mizuho Financial Group is 3.1% higher. The dollar is at 158.76 yen, compared with Y158.40 as of Thursday's Tokyo stock market close. Investors are focusing on domestic bond yields and updates from the U.S.-China summit meeting. The Nikkei Stock Average is up 0.5% at 65836.62. (kosaku.narioka@wsj.com; @kosakunarioka)

2155 GMT - Australian stocks look set to fall again in early trading amid fighting in the Middle East that pushed U.S. Treasury yields to fresh multiyear highs. ASX futures are down by 0.3% ahead of Friday's open, suggesting that the S&P/ASX 200 will add to its 0.7% decline of the previous session. With economists and traders increasingly expecting global banks to keep raising interest rates, the Australian index is down by 4.1% in September. It is on track for a fourth weekly decline, which would be its worst such streak in 10 months. In the U.S., the DJIA fell 0.3%, while the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite closed little changed. (stuart.condie@wsj.com)
